4010:
A generation after Paul wrote 1 Corinthians, the Corinthian church split again: some members removed their presbyters (elders) from office. The church in Rome wrote to urge them to repent and restore them. The letter does not name its author, but from the second century onwards it was credited to Clement, an early leader (later counted as a bishop) of Rome; Dionysius of Corinth around 170 says the letter was still read aloud in his church. It is a long sermon-like letter that strings together Old Testament examples of jealousy, repentance, faith and humility, appeals to the deaths of Peter and Paul as recent martyrs, uses the orderliness of creation and of the Roman army as models, and argues that the apostles appointed leaders and arranged for their succession.

1 Clement is copied in Codex Alexandrinus (fifth century) right after Revelation, together with 2 Clement, and in one twelfth-century Syriac New Testament manuscript after the Catholic Letters. So for some churches it stood very near the canon. But it never claims apostolic authority, and the wider church came to treat it as a precious early letter rather than Scripture.
4011: Greeting and praise of the Corinthians' former good order (chs. 1-3)
4012: Examples of the damage done by jealousy, from Cain to the deaths of Peter and Paul (chs. 4-6)
4013: Calls to repentance, hospitality and humility with Old Testament examples (chs. 7-19)
4014: Harmony in creation; the certainty of the resurrection (the phoenix illustration) (chs. 20-26)
4015: Faith and works; Christ the high priest (chs. 27-39)
4016: Order in worship and the apostles' appointment of leaders (chs. 40-44)
4017: Love as the bond of the church; Paul's earlier letter recalled (chs. 45-58)
4018: A long closing prayer, including prayer for rulers (chs. 59-65)
4019: It was never thought to be written by an apostle, and the letter itself speaks of the apostles as figures of the previous generation. Its authority came from being a respected letter of the Roman church, not a witness to Jesus. Most canon lists, including Athanasius in 367, do not include it. A few did: the *Apostolic Canons* (canon 85, late fourth century) lists two letters of Clement among New Testament books, and the Orthodox Council in Trullo (692) endorsed those canons along with other lists - so its place hovered at the edge in the East. Today all traditions treat it as a revered early writing, not Scripture. (In the Ethiopian church a different work called *Qalementos* stands in the broader canon; it is not this letter.)
4020: It is the earliest Christian document outside the New Testament that is firmly datable, so it is crucial evidence for how early believers read the Old Testament, remembered Peter and Paul, and organised leadership. Catholic writers point to it as an early example of the Roman church intervening in another church; Protestant writers note that it speaks of presbyter-bishops as a plural group, not a single monarchical bishop. Its prayer for rulers (chs. 60-61) is a model of Christian intercession under a pagan empire.
4021: Written by the Roman church, traditionally by Clement, who later tradition (Irenaeus, Origen) linked to the apostles; not itself apostolic.
4022: Around AD 96 on most views - as early as some New Testament books.
4023: Fully orthodox and widely praised for its teaching.

4050: 2 Clement is not really a letter and was not written by Clement. It is the oldest complete Christian sermon we have outside the New Testament, probably from the mid-100s. It urges listeners to repent, to keep their baptism pure and to live in light of the coming judgement.
4051:
Though called "the second letter of Clement" because it was copied after 1 Clement, this work is a sermon read aloud to a congregation (it says the speaker is reading after "the God of truth" has been read, 19.1). Its preacher urges hearers to think rightly about Christ "as about God", to show their gratitude by obeying his commands, to repent while there is time, and to "keep the flesh pure" because the body will be raised. It quotes Jesus' sayings - some like the canonical Gospels, some not found there, including a saying about the kingdom coming "when the two shall be one" that resembles material in the Gospel of Thomas and the Gospel of the Egyptians.

It survives in Codex Alexandrinus (incomplete), in the 1056 manuscript that also preserved the Didache, and in Syriac. Eusebius already doubted that it was Clement's and noted that earlier writers did not use it.

4053: Confess him by doing what he says, not only by calling him Lord (chs. 3-4)

4059: The church knew early that it was not by Clement: Eusebius remarks that it was not known as recognised like the first letter and that the ancients did not use it (*Church History* 3.38.4). It has no apostolic author, was not widely read, and quotes sayings of Jesus from sources outside the four Gospels. Its only route toward the canon was riding along with 1 Clement in a few manuscripts and in the *Apostolic Canons*, so its status stands or falls with that letter.
4060: It is the earliest surviving full Christian sermon after the New Testament and shows how a second-century preacher applied the words of Jesus. Early in it (2.4) the preacher quotes a saying of Jesus with the words "another Scripture says", one of the first times a Gospel saying is called Scripture. Catholic readers know it from the Office of Readings.

4062: Second century - early, but after the apostolic generation.

4083: The Epistle of Barnabas is a second-century treatise that reads the Old Testament as a hidden picture of Christ and argues the Jewish people misunderstood their own laws. It was copied in one of the oldest complete Bibles, Codex Sinaiticus, right after Revelation. The church valued it but recognised that Paul's companion Barnabas did not write it.
4084:
This anonymous work was credited to Barnabas, Paul's missionary partner, by Clement of Alexandria and others. It has two parts. The first (chs. 1-17) argues that God's covenant was never really given to Israel because they broke it at Sinai, and that the food laws, sacrifices, circumcision, Sabbath and Temple were always meant spiritually: the forbidden pig stands for people who remember God only when hungry, the scapegoat points to Jesus, and Abraham's 318 servants hide the cross and the name Jesus in Greek numerals. The second part (chs. 18-20) is a Two Ways teaching very like the Didache's.

Its date comes from 16.3-4, which mentions the Temple destroyed and now being rebuilt by the enemies' servants - probably Hadrian's plans in the 130s. Its sharp anti-Jewish reading of Scripture was shared by few earlier writers to the same extent and is widely criticised today.
4085: Greeting; the need for knowledge (gnosis) alongside faith (ch. 1)
4086: God does not want sacrifices or fasts but a contrite heart (chs. 2-3)
4087: The covenant broken at Sinai; the last times (ch. 4)
4088: Christ's suffering foretold; the scapegoat and red heifer (chs. 5-8)
4089: Circumcision of the heart; 318 as the cross and the name of Jesus (ch. 9)
4091: Baptism and the cross in the prophets (chs. 11-12)
4092: Who inherits the covenant; the Sabbath and the eighth day; the true Temple (chs. 13-16)
4093: The Two Ways of light and darkness (chs. 18-21)
4094: It was not by the apostle Barnabas: it was written after AD 70 (it describes the Temple destroyed) and its view of the Law conflicts with the New Testament picture of Barnabas and Paul. Eusebius classed "the so-called Epistle of Barnabas" with the "spurious" books (3.25), and it is missing from Athanasius' list. Its extreme claim that the Sinai covenant was never Israel's also cut against the New Testament's teaching that the covenants and promises belong to Israel. (Status values here mean "not in the canon"; Catholic and Orthodox readers still treat it as an early patristic text, and it is read in the Catholic Office of Readings.)
4095: Its presence in Codex Sinaiticus shows that in fourth-century Egypt some Christians still copied it with Scripture. It is an early example of reading the whole Old Testament as pointing to Christ (typology), it witnesses to Sunday as "the eighth day" of resurrection, and its Two Ways section links it with the Didache. It also condemns abortion and infanticide (19.5).
4096: Attributed to Barnabas from the late second century, but its date and content rule him out.
4097: Early second century or late first - early, but after the apostles.

4124: The Shepherd of Hermas is a long book of visions, commands and parables from second-century Rome. A Christian named Hermas is shown by an old woman (the church) and an angel dressed as a shepherd that believers who have sinned after baptism can still repent - once. It was so popular that it was copied in Codex Sinaiticus and some called it Scripture, but the church decided it was good reading rather than part of the Bible.
4125:
Hermas, a freed slave and businessman in Rome, tells of five visions, twelve "mandates" (commandments) and ten "similitudes" (parables). In the visions an elderly woman, who grows younger as the church repents, shows him a great tower being built from stones - believers - some fitting, some rejected or set aside for later. Then an angel of repentance appears dressed as a shepherd and gives commandments on faith, purity, truthfulness, patience and avoiding "double-mindedness". The parables include the elm tree and the vine (rich and poor helping each other) and a long allegory of a vineyard servant who represents God's Son.

The book's central message is that there is one more chance for repentance for Christians who have fallen after baptism, before the tower is finished. It was the most widely copied non-canonical Christian book of the early centuries: more early papyrus fragments survive of Hermas than of many New Testament books. Its view of Christ is unusual and much debated - in places it seems to identify the Son with the Holy Spirit or with a chief angel.
4126: Visions 1-4: Hermas' sins, the elderly woman (the church), the tower, the beast of coming persecution
4127: Vision 5: the angel of repentance appears as a shepherd
4128: Mandates 1-12: believe in one God; be simple; tell the truth; purity; patience; the two angels in each person; fear God; self-control; avoid double-mindedness and grief; test prophets; resist evil desire
4129: Similitudes 1-10: citizens of two cities; the elm and the vine; trees in winter and summer; true fasting; the servant in the vineyard; the shepherd of luxury; the willow tree; the great tower and the twelve mountains
4130: Its own church knew it was recent. The Muratorian fragment (usually dated to the late second century, by some to the fourth) says Hermas wrote it "very recently, in our times" while his brother Pius was bishop of Rome, so it may be read but not publicly in church among the prophets or apostles. Tertullian, after he joined the strict Montanist movement, rejected it scornfully for offering forgiveness to adulterers (*On Modesty* 10, 20). Eusebius listed it as "spurious" (3.25), and Athanasius put it among books to be read, not the canon. Its unclear Christology may also have made later teachers cautious. (A complete Ethiopic translation survives, so Ethiopian Christians read it; its exact standing there is uncertain.)
4131: Origen thought it "very useful and, I think, divinely inspired". It shaped the church's early thinking on repentance after baptism and was used to teach converts. Its pictures - the tower, the elm and the vine - became classic illustrations of the church and of rich and poor depending on each other. Historians use it to study Christian life, wealth and prophecy in second-century Rome.
4132: Not by an apostle; Hermas presents himself as a later Roman believer. Origen guessed he was the Hermas of Romans 16:14, which most doubt.
4133: Second century, after the apostolic period - which is exactly why the Muratorian fragment excluded it.
4134: Mostly orthodox in ethics, but its unclear teaching on the Son and Spirit troubled later readers.
4135: Read in Rome, Gaul, North Africa and Egypt - one of the most widespread Christian books of its day.
4136: Read privately and in catechesis; Irenaeus and Clement of Alexandria quote it as Scripture, but Rome itself refused public liturgical reading.

4164: Written in Smyrna and Troas by the bishop of Antioch in Syria, on his way to execution in Rome
4165: Ignatius was bishop of Antioch, arrested and taken to Rome to be killed by wild animals around AD 110. On the journey he wrote seven short, passionate letters to churches. He urges them to stay united around their bishop, to reject teachers who say Jesus only seemed to have a body, and he begs the Roman Christians not to stop his martyrdom.
4166:
Under armed guard, Ignatius was escorted across Asia Minor. In Smyrna he wrote to the churches of Ephesus, Magnesia and Tralles and to Rome; in Troas to Philadelphia, Smyrna and its bishop Polycarp. Three ideas dominate. First, unity: each church should do nothing without its bishop, with the presbyters and deacons; Ignatius is the first writer to describe a single bishop over each city church. Second, the reality of Christ: against "docetists" who said Jesus only appeared to suffer, he insists Jesus was truly born of Mary, truly ate and drank, truly was crucified and raised in the flesh, and he calls the eucharist "the medicine of immortality". Third, martyrdom: he longs to imitate Christ's suffering and to be "ground as God's wheat by the teeth of beasts".

The letters survive in three forms: a short Syriac version (three letters), the "middle recension" (the seven letters Eusebius knew), and a "long recension" padded out in the fourth century with six forged letters. Since the work of J. B. Lightfoot and Theodor Zahn in the nineteenth century, most scholars accept the middle seven as genuine, though a minority still question them.
4167: To the Ephesians: unity with the bishop; Christ the one physician, born and unborn
4168: To the Magnesians: do not live by Judaism; keep the Lord's Day
4169: To the Trallians: against docetism - Jesus truly suffered
4170: To the Romans: do not prevent my martyrdom
4171: To the Philadelphians: one eucharist, one altar, one bishop
4172: To the Smyrnaeans: the risen Christ ate and drank; the first use of "catholic church"

4174: No one thought these letters were Scripture. Ignatius himself draws the line: he says he does not give orders "like Peter and Paul", because they were apostles and he is a condemned man (*Romans* 4.3). They were valued as the letters of a martyr bishop, read and collected (Polycarp gathered them), but they were never put in canon lists. "Read-not-canon" here means honoured as a Father of the church; a Syriac abridgement circulated in the Syriac-speaking church.
4175: They are central evidence for second-century church structure (one bishop, presbyters, deacons), for early belief that Jesus is God ("our God, Jesus the Christ"), for the real presence of Christ in the eucharist, and for the earliest use of the phrase "catholic church" (*Smyrnaeans* 8.2). Catholic and Orthodox writers stress the bishop's role; Protestants note that Ignatius argues for an arrangement that was apparently not yet universal - his letter to Rome mentions no bishop there. All traditions honour him as a martyr.
4176: Ignatius explicitly says he is not an apostle.

4201: Polycarp was bishop of Smyrna and, according to Irenaeus, a disciple of the apostle John. He wrote this short letter to the church at Philippi, the same church Paul wrote to, giving moral advice, warning against false teaching and love of money, and sending them the letters of Ignatius. It is packed with quotations from New Testament books.
